inputs.question: What's driving reefer spot rates out of the Southeast this quarter, and what does it mean for our produce shippers?

outputs.reference: Southeast reefer spot rates averaged $2.87/mile in Q3 2026, up 14% from $2.52 in Q2. Drivers: a produce season that ran three weeks longer (cool, wet spring), Hurricane Corinne closing the Port of Savannah for four days and stranding ~1,100 reefer trailers, and ~6% of small reefer fleets leaving since January. For produce shippers, spring contract rates are well below market and tender acceptance fell to 78%, pushing loads to spot; the desk recommends reopening Q4 contract rates with the top 20 produce shippers, a separate reefer fuel surcharge line, and booking holiday produce 72 hours ahead.

inputs.question: Summarize the broker transparency rule and what Ridgeline must change.

outputs.reference: Brokers must keep an electronic record of every brokered transaction for at least three years (shipper payment, carrier payment, accessorials) and provide it electronically within 48 hours when a party to the transaction asks. Carrier waiver clauses are no longer allowed. Effective February 1, 2027 (August 1, 2027 for brokers under 10 employees; Ridgeline has 140 so Feb 1 applies). Fines up to $10,000 per violation. Ridgeline should remove waiver clauses from carrier agreements, make its TMS store shipper and carrier payments on the same load record, and set up a 48-hour request process.

inputs.question: What did the fall carrier survey say about reefer carriers shrinking or leaving the market, and why?

outputs.reference: Of reefer carriers surveyed, 22% plan to reduce fleet size in the next six months, 9% are considering leaving reefer for dry van, and only 11% plan to add trucks. Reasons: insurance premiums (64% of those shrinking), equipment financing costs (51%), and unpaid detention (47%).

inputs.question: How much have Southeast diesel prices moved since July, and roughly what does that add to our fuel surcharge per mile?

outputs.reference: Southeast retail diesel averaged $3.94/gallon in the week of October 6, 2026, up 31 cents from $3.63 in early July. Under a typical table (1 cent per mile per 6-cent diesel rise) that is roughly 5 cents more per mile in surcharge. Reefer units also burn about 0.8 gallons per hour while cooling.

inputs.question: Which of our produce shippers are driving detention costs, and how much are we paying?

outputs.reference: Ridgeline paid $41,800 in produce detention in September 2026, up from $23,500 in June. Three shippers were 58% of it: Okefenokee Fresh Farms (4.6h average dwell, $11,200), Sunbelt Pepper Co. (3.9h, $7,900) and Gator Grove Citrus (3.4h, $5,150). Only 62% was billed back because the rest lacked signed BOL in/out times. Recommendation: appointment confirmations and enforcing signed BOL times.

inputs.question: What general rate increases are LTL carriers planning for 2027?

outputs.reference: Five of the largest LTL carriers announced 2027 GRIs of 4.9% to 6.5%, median 5.9%. Accessorials are rising faster (liftgate fees up about 9%, two carriers adding a residential delivery surcharge). Shippers under 50 LTL shipments a month usually pay the full GRI; larger shippers negotiate it down one to three points.

inputs.question: Under the food traceability requirement, what do we as a broker have to keep or provide on produce loads?

outputs.reference: Brokers and carriers that only transport the food don't have to keep traceability lot codes, but must be able to provide shipping documents within 24 hours when a shipper or receiver asks during a recall. Shippers and receivers record the key data elements (lot code, quantity, from/to locations). Temperature records aren't required by the rule, though many receivers ask for reefer temperature logs contractually. Covered foods include tomatoes, peppers, leafy greens, melons and fresh-cut fruit.

inputs.question: How did our carriers' on-time performance change in Q3, especially on reefer?

outputs.reference: On-time pickup fell to 93.1% in Q3 2026 from 95.4% in Q2 and on-time delivery to 91.8% from 94.0%. Reefer on-time delivery fell to 87.2% from 92.5% (hurricane disruption and longer produce dwell). Reefer carrier fall-off rose to 4.4% from 2.1%. 37 carriers were removed from the approved list, mostly for lapsed insurance.
